lines.text: Castles on the hills, silver in the mountains and a thousand years under other crowns, until a small nation found its own way. This is the story of Slovakia.
In the eight hundreds Great Moravia rose, the first great Slavic state of Central Europe, where the brothers Cyril and Methodius came to preach.
On the Danube grew Bratislava, once called Pressburg, where Hungarian kings would be crowned for three hundred years.
For a thousand years the land was part of the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the eleven hundreds Spis Castle rose, one of the largest in Central Europe.
In the hills, Banska Stiavnica grew rich on silver, and later gave the world one of the first schools of mining.
Above the Danube, Bratislava Castle was rebuilt in the fourteen hundreds, its square shape still the city's landmark.
Then a darker tale. Countess Elizabeth Bathory was accused of murdering many girls at her castle of Cachtice, and was walled up there until she died.
Juraj Janosik, a highwayman of the mountains, was hanged young, and remembered ever after as Slovakia's Robin Hood.
Milan Rastislav Stefanik, astronomer and general, worked abroad in the First World War to found a new state of Czechs and Slovaks.
Jozef Tiso, a priest, would lead a Slovak state allied with Nazi Germany, and be executed for it in 1947.
In 1918, out of the ruins of Austria-Hungary, Czechoslovakia was born, and Slovaks and Czechs shared one country.
Alexander Dubcek, a Slovak, would one day lead the Prague Spring, a brief hope for socialism with a human face.
But in 1939, as Hitler broke Czechoslovakia apart, a separate Slovak State was set up, allied with Nazi Germany.
In 1944 Slovaks rose against the Nazis in the Slovak National Uprising. It was crushed, but it is honoured to this day.
Robert Fico, born in 1964, would serve as prime minister more than once, and survive an attempt on his life.
Zuzana Caputova, a lawyer, would become the country's first woman president in 2019.
In November 1989 students began the Velvet Revolution, and within weeks one-party communist rule had peacefully ended.
Peter Sagan, born a year later, would become a cycling star and win the world championship three times in a row.
In 1992 Czechs and Slovaks agreed to part, peacefully, without a shot fired.
On the first of January 1993 Slovakia became an independent country for the first time in modern history.
In 2004 it joined NATO and, with nine other countries, the European Union.
In 2018 the journalist Jan Kuciak and his fiancee were murdered. Huge protests followed, and the government fell.
And in May 2024, Prime Minister Robert Fico was shot, and survived.
From Great Moravia to a free Slovakia, a small nation's story continues.
